items.col_c: Use public blueprint objectives as the source of truth
items.col_d: Keep study notes tied to Cisco's published ENCOR blueprint, official documentation, course labs, and your own practice results. Avoid notes based on remembered exam content or private testing details.

items.col_c: Turn reports into broad study categories only
items.col_d: If a community post says a topic felt important, translate that into a general blueprint area to review. Do not preserve exact item wording, task lists, device roles, scoring claims, or timing claims from someone's exam attempt.

items.col_c: Do not collect or memorize disclosed exam content
items.col_d: Remove anything framed around remembered live exam content, exact task disclosure, answer patterns, scoring claims, or private test-center details. Those details can cross Cisco NDA lines and make prep less honest anyway.

items.col_c: Practice skills, not recognition
items.col_d: Use labs to build troubleshooting speed and command fluency. The goal is to solve unfamiliar network problems from fundamentals, not recognize a leaked scenario.

items.col_c: Study from the ENCOR domains
items.col_d: Balance architecture, virtualization, infrastructure, network assurance, security, automation, and AI topics according to the published blueprint. Use weak areas from practice tests to decide what gets extra time.

items.col_c: Build repeatable configuration and verification habits
items.col_d: For every lab topic you study, practice a clean loop: read requirements, plan the config, apply it, verify with show/debug/API output, break one thing, and troubleshoot it back to working.

items.col_c: Explain why each command or design choice works
items.col_d: After a lesson or lab, write a one-paragraph explanation in your own words. If you cannot explain the control plane, data plane, or failure mode, revisit the source material before moving on.

items.col_c: Interleave topics after first pass learning
items.col_d: Shuffle practice across routing, switching, assurance, security, and automation so you can identify problem types without being cued by the chapter you just studied.

items.col_c: Use legal lab sources
items.col_d: Stick to official Cisco labs, reputable courses, your own CML/EVE-NG/GNS3 topologies, and practice scenarios you create from blueprint objectives. Avoid materials that claim to reproduce live assessment content.

items.col_c: Practice verification as much as configuration
items.col_d: Build a habit of proving that a feature works: inspect neighbor state, routes, policies, counters, telemetry, API responses, logs, and failure symptoms. Verification skill transfers better than memorized command blocks.

items.col_c: Add troubleshooting reps
items.col_d: After a successful lab, intentionally introduce safe misconfigurations and recover from them. Focus on reading outputs and forming hypotheses before changing configs.

items.col_c: Practice under time pressure without chasing leaked timing details
items.col_d: Use timed practice blocks to build calm execution. Track your own time per task and improve bottlenecks instead of relying on community claims about current exam timing or section order.

items.col_c: Use practice exams diagnostically
items.col_d: Treat Boson, Pearson, course quizzes, and flashcards as feedback tools. Review every miss, explain the underlying concept, and avoid answer memorization.

items.col_c: Make flashcards from concepts and mistakes
items.col_d: Prefer cards that ask you to explain behavior, compare technologies, interpret outputs, or choose a next troubleshooting step. Avoid cards based on remembered test wording.

items.col_c: Keep a clean mistake log
items.col_d: For each missed question or failed lab, capture the objective, what you misunderstood, the correct reasoning, and a follow-up drill. That log is more useful than community rumor tracking.

items.col_c: Use the last week for synthesis
items.col_d: Revisit weak blueprint areas, redo representative labs from scratch, skim official docs for fuzzy features, and sleep enough. Do not spend the final stretch chasing community rumor threads.
